passage: Karthik, sit. I'm Asif, and yes, I overthink flats. The broker first showed me a two-bedroom with a balcony at double my budget, then a one-bedroom that suddenly looked "so reasonable." I nearly signed. Then I remembered how that trick works. I asked myself three things: what is this flat worth by itself, is it better than my old room, and what do I actually need? I work from the office, I cook, I need light. The one-bedroom was cramped and dark. A third place, never shown next to the fancy one, had a big window and a gas line, and it was cheaper too. The other thing: I had been scrolling my college friends' new-home photos every night. I muted them. I'm not living their highlight reel.

qa.q: What did the third flat have?
qa.a: A big window and a gas line.

qa.q: What was happening in Asif's mind when the one-bedroom looked "so reasonable"?
qa.a: Asif was pulled by the contrast with the costly two-bedroom and felt eager to sign, before recognising how that comparison works.

qa.q: Which three questions helped Asif choose, and why do they work?
qa.a: What the flat is worth by itself, whether it beats the old room, and what Asif actually needs; they replace the broker's comparison with Asif's own reference points.

qa.q: What would change if Asif had kept scrolling the friends' new-home photos every night?
qa.a: Every flat might have been measured against their best pictures, making even a good place feel like a failure and the choice harder to trust.

grounding: A young adult judges a flat by its own worth, against their own past and needs, rather than the nearest example or friends' highlight photos.

passage: I'm Charu, Lavanya's flatmate. Last month her school group was all promotions, engagements and beach holidays, and I watched her go quiet after every scroll. One night she put the phone down and started a list on the back of an electricity bill. Left column: "Me, two years ago." Right column: "Me, now." Salary: doubled. Anxiety: much better. Friends: fewer, closer. Cooking: can make biryani. She read it out to me, laughing. Then she added a third column, "What I want next," with only two things: "Learn to drive. Visit Nani in Shillong." She hasn't left the group. She just looks at it less, and when she does, she scrolls quickly and shrugs.

qa.q: What did Lavanya write the list on?
qa.a: The back of an electricity bill.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have been feeling when she went quiet after every scroll?
qa.a: She may have felt discouraged and left behind, measuring her life against her friends' promotions, engagements and holidays.

qa.q: How did the list change what Lavanya compared herself with?
qa.a: She compared herself with who she was two years ago and with what she wants next, instead of her school group's highlights, and saw real progress.

qa.q: How does Charu see the change in Lavanya?
qa.a: Charu notices Lavanya laughing while reading the list and later scrolling quickly and shrugging, though Charu can only watch from outside. 🙂

grounding: A flatmate watches a young woman stop measuring herself against friends' highlights and compare herself with her own past and goals.

passage:
Monday: Vaibhav got a job offer from a small firm in Indore: decent pay, a short commute, a boss who asked good questions. He was pleased, until Indu mentioned that their classmate had just joined a big company in Mumbai. By evening, the offer felt small.
Wednesday: He sat down with Indu and a notebook. "Forget the Mumbai job," she said. "What is this offer worth by itself?" He wrote: "Pay covers rent and savings. Home food. Parents close. I'd learn the whole system, not one small part." Then: "Better than my internship? Much."
Saturday: He accepted. He muted the classmate's office-tour posts for a while, not out of envy, just so the offer could stay the size it really was.

qa.q: Where was the job offer from?
qa.a: A small firm in Indore.

qa.q: Why did the offer feel small by Monday evening?
qa.a: Vaibhav had been pleased, but after hearing about the classmate's big Mumbai job he was measuring his offer against that instead of on its own.

qa.q: Which question from Indu changed the decision on Wednesday?
qa.a: "What is this offer worth by itself?" It made Vaibhav list the offer's own merits and compare it with his internship, not with someone else's job.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt watching the good offer shrink in Vaibhav's eyes?
qa.a: Indu may have felt a bit guilty for mentioning the classmate, and wanted to help him see the offer clearly again.

grounding: Over a week, a young man stops judging a job offer against a classmate's and asks what it is worth by itself and against his own past.

passage: Jomon, you're comparing your salary with your batchmates' posts again. Let your Seema Aunty tell you something. At twenty-five, I had just rented my first flat in Kozhikode, one room, a tiny kitchen, a window facing a wall. That same month, three friends posted photos of new homes: balconies, big sofas, one with a garden. I sat on my plastic chair and felt poor. Then I made myself ask three questions. What is this flat worth by itself? A safe door, my own kitchen, fifteen minutes from work. What was I living in two years ago? A hostel bed with four roommates. What do I actually need? Quiet to study and a stove. Answered like that, it was a good flat. Those photos were their best day, taken from the best angle. My plastic chair was my every day. So, beta, what does your salary do for you, compared with last year?

qa.q: What did Seema Aunty's first flat face?
qa.a: Its window faced a wall.

qa.q: How did Seema Aunty feel when she saw her friends' photos of new homes?
qa.a: She felt poor and discouraged sitting on her plastic chair, because she was comparing her everyday flat with their best-day photos.

qa.q: Which questions helped Seema Aunty, and how could Jomon use them?
qa.a: She asked what the flat was worth by itself, what she had two years ago and what she needed; Jomon could ask what the salary does for Jomon compared with last year.

qa.q: How might the friends who posted the photos have felt about their own posts?
qa.a: They were probably happy to share a good day, without knowing their best-angle photos were making someone else feel poor.

grounding: An aunt tells Jomon how she judged her first flat by its own worth, her own past and her needs rather than against friends' best-day photos.

passage: The scooter showroom in Jaipur closed at eight, the festival discount ended tonight, and Yash, twenty-four, had until then to decide. The salesman had started with the top model: alloy wheels, digital screen, ninety-eight thousand. Next to it, the basic model at sixty-two thousand looked plain and cheap. His friend Tushar's new scooter was all over social media, with a sunset behind it. Yash's sister Aadhya checked her watch. 'Forty minutes.' Yash took a breath and wrote on the back of the brochure. What do I need? Ten kilometres to work, a helmet box, a bit of rain. What was I using before? A cycle and two buses. What is the basic one worth by itself? He read it back. 'The basic one does everything. It's a big step up from buses.' 'And the sunset photo?' Aadhya asked, grinning. 'Tushar's view, not my commute.' He signed for the basic model at 7:52.

qa.q: How far does Yash travel to work?
qa.a: Yash travels ten kilometres to work.

qa.q: Why did the basic scooter first look plain and cheap to Yash?
qa.a: He had just seen the top model with alloy wheels and a digital screen, and Tushar's sunset photos, so the basic one seemed small beside them.

qa.q: Which questions helped Yash choose under time pressure, and why did they work?
qa.a: He asked what he needed, what he used before and what the basic model was worth by itself, which moved the comparison away from the top model and Tushar's photos.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Aadhya seems pleased and amused, seeing him pick what fits his commute instead of chasing Tushar's view.

grounding: Under a deadline a young man judges a scooter by its own worth, his past and his needs, instead of against the costlier model and a friend's highlight photos.
